sections.h2: Why is the Town of Oyster Bay unusual among Long Island towns?
sections.html:
It is the easternmost of Nassau County's three towns and the only one running from the Long Island Sound shore to the South Shore, about 169.5 square miles in all, with roughly 38 percent of that area water. The North Shore is hilly, the South Shore has sandy beaches and a plain fills the middle (Wikipedia).

Within the town lie 18 villages and 18 hamlets, served by 20 post offices and 30 ZIP codes. Each post office shares a name with one of those places, but the boundaries usually do not match, so your mailing address may not name the village or hamlet your lot is in. Start with the section, block and lot on your tax bill and ask the town whether your house falls inside a village.

English settlers made their first land purchase here in 1653, the settlement received its charter in 1667, and Nassau County came into being in 1899, a year after western Queens County joined New York City. Sagamore Hill, the former residence of Theodore Roosevelt, stands in the village of Cove Neck and is now a museum.

sections.h2: What kind of owners and prices does the Census record in Oyster Bay?
sections.html:
QuickFacts estimates 301,115 residents for July 2025 across 100,559 households. Owners occupy 89.1 percent of homes, a typical owned home is valued at $708,600 and renters pay a median of $2,572 a month (Census Bureau).

  • Middle household income: $160,126 in 2024 dollars
  • Monthly cost for owners with a mortgage: $3,910
  • Bachelor's degree or more among adults 25 and older: 55.6 percent
  • Residents who had not moved in the past year: 93.3 percent
  • Commute: 34.9 minutes on average

Because nearly nine in ten homes are lived in by their owners, ask your lender for a payoff figure early in any sale.

sections.h2: What does the Oyster Bay Receiver of Taxes expect, and when?
sections.html:
Two bills arrive each year, a school bill mailed in October and a general bill mailed in January, and each splits into halves. The Receiver of Taxes lists the penalty-free windows below. Owners with an escrow account have the bills sent to their lender (Receiver of Taxes FAQ).

BillDuePaid without penalty through
General tax, first halfJanuary 1February 10
General tax, second halfJuly 1August 10
School tax, first halfOctober 1November 10
School tax, second halfApril 1May 10

Source: Town of Oyster Bay Receiver of Taxes.

A late payment draws a 1 percent monthly penalty counted back to the original due date. When collection closes, on May 31 for school bills and August 31 for general bills, unpaid amounts move to the Nassau County Treasurer, and the word Arrears in the upper left corner of a bill shows that has happened. The office accepts payments at Town Hall North in Oyster Bay and Town Hall South in Massapequa, by mail and online, and only a United States Postal Service postmark proves a mailed payment was on time.

New owners should tell the Receiver in writing so the next bill reaches them. Banks, title companies and attorneys paying on someone else's behalf owe a $10 duplicate bill fee with each payment, a point to raise when the closing statement is drafted.

sections.h2: Where does an Oyster Bay owner file an assessment complaint?
sections.html:
With Nassau County, by March 1. The state tax department says the county's Assessment Review Commission meets through the year but takes complaints only until that date, and for Nassau properties it sends owners to the commission for forms and instructions (tax.ny.gov). That calendar differs from the spring Grievance Day that town boards hold elsewhere in New York.

The Receiver's FAQ notes that home improvements may alter an assessment through the Nassau County Department of Assessment in Mineola. If you added a dormer, finished a basement or built a deck, a buyer's tax bill may end up different from yours, so ask the county for the figure on file and compare it with the work you did.

sections.h2: What does the Nassau County Clerk require before it will record a deed?
sections.html:
The clerk's Land Recording Guide for the office at 240 Old Country Road in Mineola puts the property's section, block and lot first. An invalid or missing number is the most common reason for rejection, and the clerk does not check it, so copy it from the current county tax bill (Land Recording Guide).

  • Documents must be notarized, legible and signed in original ink, with party names matching exactly between the heading and the acknowledgment.
  • Post office boxes are not accepted as addresses.
  • Transfer tax goes by certified check; recording fees can go by personal check or Visa or MasterCard.
  • Present documents at least an hour before the closing.
  • Three approved companies offer e-recording, which title firms and attorneys usually use.

Forms TP-584 and RP-5217 travel with the deed. A nonresident seller who owes estimated income tax on the gain files Form IT-2663 and pays that tax to the recording officer when the deed is filed. The guide is dated October 2022, so confirm fees on the clerk's website before the closing.

sections.h2: What transfer tax does an Oyster Bay seller face?
sections.html:
New York charges two dollars on every $500 of price, counting a partial $500 as whole, and the seller carries that by default (tax.ny.gov). A sale at the town's typical owned-home value of $708,600 rounds to $709,000, which is 1,418 slices and $2,836. The rate on the state page is only the statewide piece, so ask the Nassau County Clerk whether any county or local charge also applies to your deed.

At $1 million or more for a residence, a 1 percent mansion tax kicks in on the buyer. Read the contract anyway, since the parties may shift the base tax, and the state makes buyer and seller jointly liable when the tax goes unpaid.

sections.h2: Which disclosures and permits come up on an Oyster Bay sale?
sections.html:
An owner of a house with up to four units must sign the state's seller form and deliver it ahead of the buyer's contract signature (Real Property Law 462). With a long Sound and bay shoreline, the flood section gets close reading. It asks about FEMA floodplain and flood hazard zones, flood insurance, elevation certificates, earlier flood claims, sump pumps and water entering the building from storm surge or tidal inundation.

Building permits run through the town's Department of Planning and Development, which posts application forms at oysterbaytown.com/building. Before listing, write down past work such as pools, fences, generators and solar panels and confirm each was permitted. The form also asks about certificates of occupancy, and an unclosed permit is easier to fix before a contract than after.

sections.h2: When does a cash purchase make sense for an Oyster Bay house?
sections.html: It fits when time matters more than the top price. With no buyer lender involved, the schedule rests on payoffs, the tax steps above and recording in Mineola. Have your last tax receipt, your deed and any open permit paperwork on the table before you ask anyone for a number.

faqs.q: When does the first half of Oyster Bay's general tax come due?
faqs.a: January 1, payable without penalty through February 10. The second half falls due July 1 and is payable through August 10. The school bill keeps its own calendar, with October 1 and April 1 due dates.

faqs.q: What if I skip an Oyster Bay tax deadline?
faqs.a: A 1 percent penalty per month accrues, counted from the original due date. After May 31 for school bills and August 31 for general bills, the unpaid balance is payable to the Nassau County Treasurer in place of the Receiver of Taxes.

faqs.q: How late can I challenge an Oyster Bay assessment?
faqs.a: March 1. The state tax department says Nassau County's Assessment Review Commission accepts complaints through that date. Ask the commission for the forms, since the state page points Nassau owners there.

faqs.q: Which number must appear on a Nassau County deed?
faqs.a: The section, block and lot, plus a unit number for a condominium. The clerk's guide wants it on the first page and says to copy it from the current tax bill. Mistakes here cause more rejected filings than any other error.

faqs.q: Who pays the mansion tax when an Oyster Bay house sells for $1.2 million?
faqs.a: The buyer. The mansion tax is 1 percent of the price on a residence sold at $1 million or more, and the seller owes it only if the buyer fails to pay. The base transfer tax of $2 per $500 is the seller's by default.
